addressed_problems.content: Although lottery-ticket initializations from natural-image datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Fashion-MNIST) are known to transfer to non-natural domains in a domain-dependent manner—succeeding on digital-heritage artwork classification but showing stronger limitations on digital-pathology datasets—the mechanistic causes of this differential transferability remain unresolved. In particular, it is not understood how specific distributional differences (e.g., differences in texture, image statistics, imaging-pipeline artifacts, or biological morphology) determine whether a winning ticket contains inductive biases that are sufficiently generic to generalize to a given non-natural target. Resolving this gap would enable principled prediction of when natural-image tickets are suitable for a target domain without requiring exhaustive empirical testing.

The computational cost of discovering winning tickets via iterative pruning from a fully trained network remains high, and current approaches (e.g., using tickets from a small set of natural-image sources) do not amortize this cost across many non-natural targets. It remains unresolved whether scalable ticket-finding algorithms exist that avoid repeated full training on each source dataset or whether strategies can be developed to discover tickets that are broadly reusable across many non-natural domains without requiring per-target discovery. Addressing this open problem could make lottery-ticket transfer learning practical for applications where training data is scarce.

The findings on lottery-ticket transferability to non-natural image domains are currently limited to a ResNet-50 architecture and to classification tasks. It remains an open question whether these findings extend to other neural network architectures (e.g., VGG, DenseNet, or transformer-based vision models) and to other computer vision tasks beyond classification, such as image localization, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation—including biomedical segmentation of tissues or cells. Furthermore, it is unknown whether winning tickets found on natural images can transfer to non-natural data in other modalities (e.g., audio, text, or time series) that also suffer from data scarcity. Establishing the generality of the observed transferability patterns would significantly broaden the impact of the lottery ticket hypothesis for practical applications.

Although preliminary experiments suggest that winning tickets found on a reduced fraction (e.g., 25%) of source training data maintain robustness to large pruning rates but achieve lower final testing accuracy than tickets found on the full dataset, the relationship between source-data size, ticket sparsity level, and obtainable target accuracy has not been characterized quantitatively across different regimes. It remains unresolved how much source data is minimally required to obtain a winning ticket that yields near-optimal transfer performance on a given target domain. A formal characterization of this trade-off would guide data collection and resource allocation when applying lottery-ticket transfer learning in data-scarce settings.

The study conjectures that the stronger transferability of natural-image lottery tickets to digital-heritage datasets compared to digital-pathology datasets arises because biomedical images are distributionally further from natural images than artworks are, but this conjecture has not been formally tested. It remains an open problem to develop and validate quantitative measures of cross-domain distributional distance (e.g., based on image statistics, feature-space divergence, or other proxies) that can predict the success of lottery-ticket transfer to a given non-natural target without requiring expensive empirical evaluation. Deriving such predictive measures would provide a principled foundation for deciding when to use natural-image tickets versus when to seek tickets directly on the target domain.

The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) proposes that within large randomly initialized neural networks there exist sparse sub-networks (winning tickets) which, when trained from their initial weights, can match or exceed the performance of the original dense network. Prior empirical and theoretical work demonstrated and characterized winning tickets primarily within the natural-image classification setting (e.g., CIFAR, ImageNet) and on relatively small-scale architectures and tasks. Practical use of winning tickets for transfer learning and for data-scarce target domains remains uncertain because: (a) the LTH has not been systematically validated on non-natural image domains (such as digital pathology or artworks), so it is unknown whether similarly sparse, trainable sub-networks exist there; (b) it is unclear whether winning-ticket initializations found on natural-image datasets contain inductive biases that are generic enough to transfer to substantially different, non-natural target distributions; (c) datasets in non-natural domains are often small, which raises the practical question whether training a sparse winning-ticket model is preferable to training a larger over-parameterized model from scratch under scarce-data regimes; and (d) standard procedures to identify winning tickets (iterative training+pruning with late-resetting) are computationally expensive, so transferability across domains would be required for practical reuse. Because these uncertainties directly affect the ability to (i) obtain compact, better-regularized models for non-natural tasks, (ii) reuse a single costly-found ticket across multiple target datasets, and (iii) choose between pruning-derived sparse models and conventional transfer-learning or dense training under limited data, an empirical investigation that (1) verifies the existence and robustness of winning tickets in non-natural image datasets, (2) quantifies their performance relative to dense models trained from scratch, and (3) measures how well natural-image tickets transfer into non-natural domains is required.

nodes.content: In deep learning for image classification, the prevailing practice uses large over-parameterized convolutional networks (e.g., ResNet-50) trained end-to-end; prior LTH work had shown that many weights can be pruned without losing accuracy but this was demonstrated mainly on natural-image datasets. For non-natural image domains (histopathology, artworks) it was unknown whether comparable extreme sparsity could be achieved without degrading accuracy: if winning tickets did not exist or were fragile in these domains, then (i) model compression via pruning would be less applicable, (ii) sparse training could not be relied upon as a regularizer for small datasets, and (iii) the presumed ubiquity of redundant parameters in large architectures would be unverified for biomedical and cultural-heritage imagery. The absence of evidence meant practitioners lacked guidance on whether to search for sparse trainable sub-networks when targeting non-natural image tasks.

When training data are scarce, over-parameterized networks tend to overfit and require strong regularization or transfer learning; prior works had not established whether pruning to produce winning-ticket sparse models yields consistent gains over training a dense model from scratch on small non-natural-image datasets. If pruned winners did not reliably outperform dense training in these regimes, the utility of pursuing expensive ticket-discovery procedures would be limited. Therefore, practitioners needed empirical evidence comparing (i) sparse winning-ticket fine-tuning and (ii) training the original dense network from scratch under identical limited-data conditions to decide whether to invest in pruning workflows for non-natural imaging tasks.

Prior transferability studies of lottery tickets focused on transfers within the natural-image domain and suggested that tickets discovered on large natural datasets can generalize across related vision tasks. It remained unknown whether such transferability extends to non-natural-image domains that differ substantially in image statistics and in the kinds of discriminative cues (e.g., color/texture vs. cellular morphology). Without domain-specific evidence, it was unclear whether reusing an expensive-to-find natural-image ticket would be a reliable strategy for biomedical or cultural-heritage tasks, or whether tickets should be discovered within each target domain to maximize accuracy. The absence of such evidence left open whether domain shift reduces or preserves the inductive biases encoded by winning initializations and therefore whether cross-domain reuse is practical.

Standard transfer-learning practice often fine-tunes a pre-trained (fully trained) network or its pruned variant on a target task; the LTH literature distinguishes lottery-ticket initializations (early-iteration resets) from the alternative of transferring the end-of-training weights on the pruned structure. It was unknown whether the purported specialness of early-iteration winning initializations would hold as an advantage over end-of-training pruned initializations in cross-domain fine-tuning. This distinction matters because if fully trained pruned weights were at least as good, then finding lottery tickets would be unnecessary for transfer scenarios; conversely, if early-iteration tickets are superior, this motivates searching for and reusing late-reset tickets rather than transferring fully trained pruned weights.

The potential to reuse a ticket discovered on one non-natural dataset for a related non-natural target would reduce computation and data requirements when many related tasks exist (e.g., different biomedical cohorts or different art subsets). Prior work did not extensively evaluate intra–non-natural-domain ticket transfer, so it was unknown whether task relatedness in non-natural domains produces transferable inductive biases in winning initializations. Without this knowledge, practitioners could not assess whether to prune per-target or prune once on a related source to benefit multiple targets.

If identifying winning tickets required large source datasets, then small-target or small-source regimes would preclude ticket discovery and reuse. It was therefore important to know whether the amount of data available at ticket-discovery time controls the sparsity-robustness tradeoff: if robustness degrades sharply with less data, tickets found on small sources would be fragile. Prior work had not quantified this effect for non-natural datasets, leaving uncertainty about whether ticket discovery is feasible when only modestly sized datasets are available.

Extremely sparse sub-networks recovered via the iterative magnitude-pruning with late-resetting (where k=2, i.e., resetting unpruned weights to their values at the second epoch of the first pruning iteration) procedure on a ResNet-50 architecture preserve high classification performance on non-natural image datasets: winning-ticket models maintain good final test accuracy up to very large pruning fractions (examples include tickets that prune approximately 0.86 to 0.99 of the ResNet-50 weights while still achieving near-peak accuracy), thereby confirming that a very large fraction of the ResNet-50 parameters are superfluous for the considered digital-pathology and digital-heritage classification tasks and that the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) phenomenon extends to these non-natural-image domains.

metadata.narrative: The core existence and robustness claim is well-supported by the cross-domain replication and random-reinitialization comparison (H1). However, P1 identifies a comparative weakness in the subsidiary claim of superfluity due to the use of a scratch-training baseline rather than the full pretrained network, leaving the interpretation of overparameterization uncertain. The conclusion is credible in its primary claim but the superfluity assertion is not firmly grounded.

nodes.title: Existence and robustness of winning tickets on non-natural image datasets

nodes.content: Across all seven tested non-natural target datasets, the best-performing pruned winning-ticket model (selected among 31 sparsity levels and among tickets originating from CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion-MNIST, or the target dataset) achieves substantially higher test accuracy than a fully unpruned ResNet-50 trained from random initialization on the same target data. Numeric comparisons (mean ± std over four seeds) include: Human-LBA: best pruned 81.72±0.39 vs scratch 71.85±1.12; Lung-Tissues: 90.48±0.16 vs 84.75±0.81; Mouse-LBA: 74.20±2.04 (CIFAR-10 ticket) vs 48.17±1.18; Bone-Marrow: 72.55±0.46 vs 64.66±1.36; Artist-Classification-1: 66.58±1.54 (CIFAR-10 ticket) vs 45.88±0.42; Type-Classification: 60.56±0.44 (CIFAR-100 ticket) vs 41.36±2.31. Typical improvements are on the order of ≈10% absolute accuracy and reach ≈20% in some cases.

metadata.narrative: The qualitative advantage of pruned tickets over scratch training is robust, as shown by consistent large effect sizes across all seven datasets with multi-seed averaging (H2). Nevertheless, P3 reveals a statistical risk from post-hoc test-set selection of the best sparsity level, which inflates the reported magnitudes and makes the exact quantitative claim uncertain. The core pattern likely holds, but the reported superiority should be treated as an upper bound.

nodes.title: Pruned winning-ticket models outperform unpruned ResNet-50 trained from scratch on all seven tested non-natural target datasets

nodes.content: Winning-ticket initializations (pruned subnetworks obtained via iterative magnitude pruning with late-resetting to epoch 2 on a source dataset) found on natural-image datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion-MNIST) transfer to non-natural target datasets in a domain-dependent manner: for the digital-heritage (art) classification tasks, natural-image tickets consistently outperform tickets found by pruning on the target art datasets (e.g., Artist-Classification-1: CIFAR-10 ticket 66.58±1.54 vs target-ticket, i.e., tickets found on the target dataset itself, 58.74±1.92), while for digital-pathology (biomedical) datasets the reverse holds in most cases — target-domain winning tickets reach higher test accuracy than natural-image tickets (e.g., Human-LBA: target-ticket 81.72±0.39 vs best natural CIFAR-10 79.17±1.85; Lung-Tissues: target-ticket 90.48±0.16 vs CIFAR-10 88.90±1.97), with one exception (Mouse-LBA) where a CIFAR-10 ticket outperforms the target-ticket (74.20±2.04 vs 68.20±3.79).

metadata.narrative: The conclusion is empirically secure: the domain-dependent transferability pattern is replicated across three natural-image sources and seven target datasets with only one minor exception (H3). No load-bearing weak points were identified, so the conclusion is fully credited within the tested scope.

nodes.title: Domain-dependent transferability of natural-image winning tickets to non-natural datasets

nodes.content: For transfer to a target non-natural dataset, a pruned network initialized with an early-iteration late-reset winning initialization f(x;m⊙θk) (where f is the ResNet-50 function, x is the input, m is a binary mask obtained by iterative magnitude pruning on a source dataset, ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication, and θk are the weights at the second epoch of the first pruning iteration of the source) yields higher final accuracy and greater robustness to high pruning rates than the same pruned structure initialized with the final trained source weights f(x;m⊙θi) (where i is the last training iteration of the source). That is, pruned-but-fully-trained initializations perform worse than late-reset lottery-ticket initializations when fine-tuned on the target.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion is not adequately supported; P4 shows that the evidence is limited to a single target dataset and lacks numerical reporting. There are no highlights that meaningfully address this deficiency. The finding should be considered preliminary and requires broader validation.

nodes.title: Late-reset lottery ticket initializations outperform pruned models initialized with fully trained source weights when transferred to non-natural datasets

nodes.content: Transferring winning-ticket initializations (pruned subnetworks with weights reset to epoch 2 via iterative magnitude pruning on a source dataset) between related non-natural datasets (e.g., Human-LBA to Mouse-LBA, both from the live-blood-analysis biomedical domain; Artist-Classification-1 to Artist-Classification-2, both from the digital-heritage artist-classification domain) yields better or comparable final accuracy and improved robustness to pruning compared to transferring unrelated natural-image tickets; specifically, Human-LBA tickets perform as well as Mouse-LBA tickets on Mouse-LBA and are more robust to extreme sparsity, and Artist-Classification-1 tickets can outperform Artist-Classification-2 tickets when transferred reciprocally.

metadata.narrative: Similar to C4, the evidence rests on only two transfer pairs with visual-only presentation (P5); the limited scope and absence of quantitative support mean the conclusion cannot be considered established. No highlights offset this.

nodes.title: Transferring winning tickets between related non-natural datasets improves performance and robustness compared to natural-image tickets

nodes.content: The stability of lottery-ticket (pruned subnetwork with weights reset to epoch 2 via iterative magnitude pruning) performance under high pruning does not strongly depend on the size of the training set used to discover the ticket: winning tickets obtained from training on only 25% of the original training data yield similarly stable performance curves under increasing pruning as tickets found on the full dataset, although their final test accuracy on the target is lower than that of tickets discovered with the full training set.

metadata.narrative: The empirical support is too weak for the conclusion to be credited: the experiment is conducted on a single unspecified dataset with only visual assessment (P6). No highlights elevate the evidence. The claim remains conjectural.

nodes.title: Lottery-ticket robustness to high pruning is stable across training-set sizes, with lower peak accuracy for smaller sets

nodes.content: In the transfer-learning setting where winning tickets (pruned subnetworks of a ResNet-50 with weights reset to the second epoch of the first pruning iteration via iterative magnitude pruning) are identified on a source dataset (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion-MNIST, or the target dataset itself) and then fine-tuned on a non-natural target dataset, the test accuracy of the best pruned ticket is compared to the test accuracy of a randomly initialized, unpruned ResNet-50 trained from scratch on the same target data to support the inference that a large fraction of ResNet-50 parameters are superfluous for the target task, rather than being compared to the test accuracy of a full (unpruned) source-pretrained ResNet-50 fine-tuned on the target dataset.Table 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the unpruned source-pretrained model fine-tuned on the target achieved accuracy comparable to or higher than the best pruned ticket, then the claim that a large fraction of parameters are superfluous would be invalid; instead, the ticket's performance might simply reflect the utility of pretrained features, with sparsity providing little additional benefit beyond compression.
metadata.weakness_reason: The LTH claim for transfer should compare the sub-network (ticket) to the full network with the same initial weights (the source-pretrained full model) to determine whether parameters are superfluous. The chosen baseline (scratch training) does not share the same pretrained features, so the ticket's advantage could be due to pretrained features rather than sparsity. The paper does not report the full source-pretrained model's target accuracy, so the claim of superfluity is not justified by the presented evidence.

nodes.title: Missing baseline for superfluity claim

nodes.content: For each of the seven non-natural target datasets, the test-set accuracy reported as the best pruned winning-ticket model is obtained by examining the test-set accuracies of all 31 sparsity levels produced from a given source (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion-MNIST, or the target dataset) and selecting the highest accuracy value, without using a held-out validation set for this selection. The scratch-training baseline, in contrast, is a single ResNet-50 trained from random initialization on the target data and evaluated once on the test set, without any analogous multi-candidate selection.Table 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the selection bias were removed (e.g., by using a validation set for sparsity selection and reporting the respective test accuracy), the best pruned model's accuracy could be lower, potentially reducing or eliminating the advantage over scratch training for some datasets. For datasets with high variance (e.g., Mouse-LBA CIFAR-10 best: 74.20±2.04), the selection could account for a non-trivial fraction of the improvement, weakening the conclusion that winning tickets consistently and substantially outperform scratch training.
metadata.weakness_reason: Selecting the best among many candidates on the test set inflates the reported accuracy because the test set is used for both selection and evaluation; the standard deviation of the best-of-31 expected maximum can be substantial, especially with small test sets (e.g., 360 test samples for the art datasets). The paper does not correct for this or report validation-based selection. The scratch baseline, trained from a single random initialization without tuning, provides a statistically weaker comparison. The observed difference may therefore overstate the true advantage of winning tickets over dense training.

nodes.title: Selection bias from post-hoc test-set selection

nodes.content: The comparison between late-reset lottery tickets (defined as f(x;m⊙θk) with k=2, where f is the ResNet-50 function, x is the input, m is a binary mask obtained by iterative magnitude pruning on a source dataset, ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication, and θk are the weights at the second epoch of the first pruning iteration) and fully-trained pruned initializations (defined as f(x;m⊙θi) where i is the final training iteration of the same source model) for transfer to a non-natural target dataset is evaluated on a single target dataset from the digital-pathology domain (Human-LBA) using source tickets from CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The results are displayed as accuracy-versus-sparsity curves without reporting numerical test-set accuracies, standard deviations over the four experimental seeds, or any statistical significance test.Fig. 4, first row

metadata.failure_mode: If the experiment had been run on other target datasets and showed that fully-trained initializations perform as well as or better than late-reset tickets, the conclusion would be directly contradicted. Given the limited empirical basis, the conclusion as stated ("Lottery-ticket (late-reset) initializations outperform pruned models initialized with fully trained source weights" for transfer to a non-natural dataset) is not supported as a general claim; it is at best a preliminary observation for a specific combination of source and target.
metadata.weakness_reason: The experiment samples only one out of seven target datasets and two out of three source datasets, so it is unknown whether the conclusion generalizes to other target domains (e.g., digital heritage, other biomedical tasks) or to the Fashion-MNIST source. Furthermore, the lack of numerical reporting prevents the reader from quantifying the magnitude of the advantage or its uncertainty across seeds, making it impossible to assess whether the difference is statistically significant or consistent.

nodes.title: Single-dataset visual evidence for late-reset advantage

nodes.content: The evaluation of whether transferring lottery tickets (winning tickets defined as f(x;m⊙θk) with k=2, where f is the ResNet-50 function, x is the input, m is a binary mask obtained by iterative magnitude pruning on a source dataset, ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication, and θk are the weights at the second epoch of the first pruning iteration) between related non-natural target datasets is beneficial considers two specific pairs: (1) tickets found on the Human-LBA dataset (a live-blood-analysis biomedical dataset) and fine-tuned on the Mouse-LBA dataset (another live-blood-analysis dataset), and (2) tickets found on the Artist-Classification-1 dataset (a digital-heritage artist-classification task with 20 artists) and fine-tuned on the Artist-Classification-2 dataset (a separate digital-heritage artist-classification task with 19 artists). Results for both pairs are shown as accuracy-versus-sparsity curves without reporting numerical test-set accuracies, standard deviations, or any statistical comparison.Fig. 4, second row

metadata.failure_mode: If other related pairs were tested and showed no advantage or a disadvantage, the general conclusion that "transferring winning-ticket initializations between related non-natural datasets yields better or comparable final accuracy" would be false. Even for the tested pairs, without statistical quantification, the visual impression might not hold under replication or across different random seeds.
metadata.weakness_reason: The empirical base is too narrow to support a general claim about intra–non-natural-domain ticket transfer. The two pairs may not represent the diversity of non-natural image tasks; many other potential related pairs (e.g., Lung-Tissues to Bone-Marrow, Type-Classification to Artist-Classification) are not tested. Moreover, the lack of numerical reporting prevents readers from verifying the magnitude and reliability of the advantage, and the possibility that overlapping classes or dataset curation artifacts (in the art pair) inflate performance is not examined.

nodes.title: Limited two-pair visual evidence for intra-domain transfer

nodes.content: The experiment that reduces the training-set size used for discovering lottery tickets (winning tickets defined as f(x;m⊙θk) with k=2) on a target dataset — testing 75%, 50%, and 25% of the original training data while keeping the validation and test sets fixed — and measures the resulting sparsity-accuracy curves (accuracy vs. fraction of pruned weights) is performed on a single, unspecified non-natural target dataset from the set of seven. The stability of the curves across data-size conditions is assessed by visual inspection of overlapping plots, without numerical reporting of accuracy values, standard errors, or any quantitative measure such as the area under the sparsity-accuracy curve or the accuracy decay rate at high pruning fractions.Fig. 4, third row

metadata.failure_mode: If the experiment were replicated on other target datasets (e.g., smaller ones like Bone-Marrow with only 522 training samples) and showed that ticket robustness degrades when the discovery dataset is very small, the conclusion that stability does not depend on dataset size would be false. The current single-dataset visual evidence cannot rule out such degradation. The conclusion that "the stability of lottery-ticket performance under high pruning does not strongly depend on the size of the training set" is therefore not firmly established.
metadata.weakness_reason: The dataset identity is not disclosed, so the reader cannot assess the representativeness or connect the result to the properties of a particular dataset (e.g., size, domain, task difficulty). The use of a single dataset severely limits generalization. The absence of quantitative metrics for stability (e.g., area under the sparsity-accuracy curve, confidence intervals for accuracy at high sparsity) means the claim of "similar stability" relies on visual interpretation, which may not be robust.

nodes.title: Single-unspecified-dataset visual evidence for size-independence

nodes.content: Across all seven non-natural target datasets (Human-LBA, Lung-Tissues, Mouse-LBA, Bone-Marrow from digital pathology; Artist-Classification-1, Type-Classification, Artist-Classification-2 from digital heritage), late-reset winning tickets (found via iterative magnitude pruning with 20% per step and $k=2$ late-resetting on the respective source dataset) maintain high classification accuracy at sparsity levels ranging from 0.83 to 0.99 of the original ResNet-50 weights (Table 3 shows the best-performing sparsity level per ticket). In every case, the accuracy of these tickets is substantially higher than that of the same pruned structure with its weights randomly reinitialized (the orange curves in Fig. 3), confirming that the specific late-reset initialization, not merely the pruning mask, is responsible for the preserved accuracy.

metadata.credit: This highlight guards against the alternative explanation that any mask of high sparsity would perform well due to the pruning mask alone; by showing that random reinitialization degrades quickly, the paper demonstrates that the ticket initialization is a necessary component. The consistency across seven datasets establishes that the phenomenon is not specific to a single domain or dataset. Together, these observations provide strong support for the primary claim that winning tickets exist and are robust in non-natural image domains, establishing a factual foundation that extends the LTH beyond natural images.

nodes.title: Cross-domain replication and random-reinit comparison

nodes.content: On all seven non-natural target datasets, the best pruned winning-ticket model (selected from among 31 sparsity levels and up to four source datasets: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion-MNIST, and the target dataset itself) achieves a higher test accuracy than a randomly initialized, unpruned ResNet-50 trained from scratch on the same target data. The improvements, averaged over four random seeds and reported in Table 2, range from approximately 7% absolute (Bone-Marrow target-ticket 72.55±0.46 vs scratch 64.66±1.36) to over 26% absolute (Mouse-LBA CIFAR-10 ticket 74.20±2.04 vs scratch 48.17±1.18), with the reported standard deviations being small relative to the size of the improvement.

metadata.credit: This highlight provides multi-dataset replication with consistent effect sizes, which rules out the possibility that the advantage is a one-time artifact. The use of four seeds provides a basic measure of repeatability. The large effect sizes (≥7%, often 10–20% absolute) mean that even if the selection bias from P3 reduces the reported numbers, the qualitative conclusion of superiority over scratch training is highly likely to hold. Thus, the core comparative claim is robust, even though the precise magnitude may be overestimated.

nodes.title: Consistent large effect sizes across all datasets with multi-seed averaging

nodes.content: The domain-dependent transferability pattern is observed for all three natural-image source datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion-MNIST) across all seven non-natural target datasets. On each of the three digital-heritage (art) datasets, every natural-image source produces a best pruned ticket with higher test accuracy than the target-domain ticket (e.g., on Artist-Classification-1: CIFAR-10 66.58±1.54 vs target 58.74±1.92; CIFAR-100 65.55±1.79; Fashion-MNIST 63.88±0.12; from Table 2). On the four digital-pathology datasets, the target-domain ticket outperforms all natural-image sources on three datasets (Human-LBA, Lung-Tissues, Bone-Marrow), and the exception (Mouse-LBA) shows CIFAR-10 outperforming the target ticket (74.20±2.04 vs 68.20±3.79) while CIFAR-100 and Fashion-MNIST still trail the target ticket.

metadata.credit: This highlight demonstrates that the domain dependence is not an artifact of a particular source dataset or a single target dataset. The pattern is replicated across multiple sources and multiple targets, with the only exception (Mouse-LBA) suggesting a boundary condition rather than refuting the trend. This empirical regularity provides strong support for the conclusion that transferability is domain-dependent: natural-image tickets transfer well to artwork classification (which shares visual characteristics with natural images) but less well to biomedical classification (which differs more in image statistics). Without this multi-source, multi-target replication, the claim could be dismissed as idiosyncratic to a particular source or target.

nodes.title: Replicated domain-dependent pattern across sources and targets

steps.reasoning:
Define the model and the notion of a winning ticket used in the experiments: $f(x;\theta)$ denotes a neural network (here a ResNet-50 convolutional neural network), $\theta_0\sim\mathcal{D}_\theta$ denotes random initial parameters, $m$ denotes a binary mask that indicates which parameters are retained after pruning, and $\theta_k$ denotes the network weights at an early training iteration indexed by $k$; a late-reset winning ticket is the reparameterized pruned network $f(x;m\odot\theta_k)$ where $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication and $k=2$ was used in all experiments. This formalization of winning tickets and the choice of $k=2$ follow the late-resetting procedure described in the experimental setup.
[4]

Describe how winning tickets are obtained in the experimental procedure: start from an initial network $f(x;\theta_0)$, train it, iteratively prune by magnitude with pruning rate $0.20$ (i.e., prune the lowest-magnitude 20% of weights at each pruning iteration), repeat 31 pruning iterations to obtain 31 sparsity levels, and for each pruning iteration reset the surviving weights to the values they had at the early iteration $k=2$ to obtain tickets $f(x;m\odot\theta_k)$. The experiments use no data augmentation, SGD with initial learning rate $10^{-1}$, Nesterov momentum $\rho=0.9$, and weight decay $\alpha=10^{-5}$; early stopping halts training when validation loss does not decrease for 5 epochs.
[16]

State the transfer-and-fine-tune evaluation protocol used to measure whether winning tickets generalize to non-natural images: for each winning ticket $f(x;m\odot\theta_k)$ found on a source dataset (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 or Fashion-MNIST), replace the final linear classification layer with a randomly initialized layer that matches the number of classes $Q_t$ of the non-natural target dataset, then fine-tune the pruned network on the target training set and report final test accuracy on the target test set. Repeat experiments with four random seeds and report mean±std.
[16]

Present the empirical observation that pruned winning tickets maintain high accuracy up to very large pruning fractions: performance-vs-sparsity curves (final test accuracy on the y-axis, fraction of weights pruned on the x-axis) show that, for several target datasets, pruned winners retain near-peak accuracy even when only about $1\%$ of the original weights remain (i.e., when $\approx 0.99$ fraction is pruned), and more generally are robust across large pruning fractions. This observation is reported visually in the multi-curve plot of final performance versus pruning fraction.
Fig. 3

Support the numerical claim about extreme sparsity with specific pruning fractions observed for the best-performing tickets: the fraction of weights pruned for the best ticket per target dataset (reported as the characterizing level of sparsity) includes values such as $0.945$, $0.977$, $0.972$, $0.866$, $0.991$, $0.991$, and $0.963$ for various source–target combinations, i.e., pruning fractions in the approximate range $0.86$–$0.99$ (meaning only about $1\%$–$14\%$ of weights remain) for the reported best tickets. These numbers are reported in the table that lists pruning fractions for the best-performing winning tickets.
Table 3

Conclude that the existence of high-performing tickets at pruning fractions in the range $\approx 0.86$--$0.99$ demonstrates that a very large fraction of ResNet-50 parameters are superfluous for the considered target classification tasks: since winning tickets that retain only a small fraction of parameters still achieve near-peak accuracy on non-natural datasets, those pruned parameters are not necessary for competitive performance on these tasks.
Table 3

State the additional empirical confirmation that pruned winning-ticket models not only exist but are robust across different non-natural target domains: in the first three target datasets the performance of winning tickets "barely suffer" even when models keep only $\approx 1\%$ of original weights, while in the other datasets the winning-ticket performance begins to degrade only once $\approx 97\%$ of weights are pruned; these qualitative trends are visible in the performance-vs-sparsity curves and are reported in the Results discussion.
Fig. 3

Restate the evaluation comparison that establishes the claim: for each target dataset, the authors compare the best-performing pruned winning-ticket model (best among 31 sparsity levels and among tickets originating from CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion-MNIST, or the target dataset) to a fully unpruned ResNet-50 trained from random initialization on the same target data (referred to as "scratch" or "unpruned model trained from scratch"); experiments are repeated over four random seeds and results are reported as mean±std.
Table 2

Quantify the typical improvement magnitude observed: from the table and the discussion, typical absolute accuracy improvements are on the order of $\approx 10\%$, and in some cases reach $\approx 20\%$ (for example, Mouse-LBA and Artist-Classification-1 exhibit improvements over 20 percentage points compared to scratch). This statement is an explicit synthesis of the numeric contrasts shown in the results table and the Results text.
Table 2

Support the quantitative comparison with the visual evidence that pruned models outperform unpruned models across pruning fractions: the multi-curve plots (performance vs fraction of weights pruned) consistently show the colored lines (pruned winning-ticket models) lying above the black dashed line (unpruned model trained from scratch) across all tested datasets, indicating that pruned winners produce higher final test accuracy than the unpruned baseline throughout the sparsity sweep.
Fig. 3

Conclude that, under the scarce-data training conditions used by the experiments (dataset sizes listed in Table 1, small-to-moderate numbers of training samples per dataset), the best pruned winning-ticket models achieve substantially higher test accuracy than a fully unpruned ResNet-50 trained from random initialization on the same target data, as evidenced by the reported numeric results and plots.
Table 1

Define the classes of source tickets whose transferability is compared: "natural-image tickets" refers to winning-ticket initializations found on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, or Fashion-MNIST; "target-domain tickets" or "non-natural tickets" refers to winning tickets found by pruning on the same non-natural target dataset (i.e., winning tickets obtained by applying the iterative pruning-and-late-reset procedure directly on the target distribution).

Summarize the experimental protocol used to evaluate transferability differences: for each target dataset the authors fine-tune winning tickets found on natural-image sources as well as tickets found on the target dataset, then compare final test accuracies (mean±std over four seeds) and the robustness of performance across pruning fractions; results are visualized in the performance-vs-sparsity plots and summarized numerically in the results table.
Fig. 3
Table 2

Report the empirical pattern observed on digital-heritage (art) classification tasks: for the two artist classification tasks and the type-classification task the natural-image tickets consistently outperform tickets found on the target artistic datasets. For example, on Artist-Classification-1 the CIFAR-10 ticket achieves $66.58\pm1.54$ while the target-ticket achieves $58.74\pm1.92$, i.e., the natural-image ticket is substantially better than the target-domain ticket on this art classification task; these values are taken directly from the comparison table.
Table 2

Report the empirical pattern observed on digital-pathology (biomedical) datasets: in three out of four biomedical datasets the target-domain winning tickets outperform natural-image tickets. Specific numeric examples from the comparison table are: Human-LBA target-ticket $81.72\pm0.39$ vs best natural CIFAR-10 $79.17\pm1.85$; Lung-Tissues target-ticket $90.48\pm0.16$ vs CIFAR-10 $88.90\pm1.97$. These numbers show that, for these biomedical datasets, tickets found directly on the biomedical data reach higher test accuracy than tickets transferred from natural-image sources.
Table 2

Note the exception and mixed case: Mouse-LBA is the only biomedical dataset where a natural-image ticket outperforms the target-ticket: CIFAR-10 ticket $74.20\pm2.04$ vs target-ticket $68.20\pm3.79$, as reported in the comparison table. This demonstrates that transferability is domain-dependent and that exceptions exist.
Table 2

Relate qualitative stability-of-performance observations: besides final accuracy, the authors note that tickets found on the target (non-natural) distributions sometimes suffer more when extreme pruning rates are reached, i.e., some target-domain tickets are less stable at very high sparsity than natural-image tickets on certain datasets (an observation described in the Results and visible in the performance curves). This further indicates the domain-dependent nature of transferability.
Fig. 3

Synthesize the domain-dependent conclusion: combine the numerical comparisons and curve-based stability observations to conclude that winning-ticket initializations from natural-image datasets transfer to non-natural target datasets in a domain-dependent manner—natural-image tickets perform better on art datasets, while target-domain tickets generally perform better on biomedical datasets, with an explicit exception (Mouse-LBA) where a natural ticket outperforms the target ticket.

Define the two initialization schemes compared in the transfer experiments: (a) lottery-ticket late-reset initializations $f(x;m\odot\theta_k)$ where $\theta_k$ are weights obtained at an early iteration $k$ (with $k=2$ used in all experiments), and (b) pruned networks initialized with fully trained source weights $f(x;m\odot\theta_i)$ where $\theta_i$ denotes the weights at the final training iteration $i$ of the source task. These definitions are explicitly given in the Additional Studies experimental description.

Describe the experiment that compares these initializations: take a pruned structure (mask $m$) obtained by pruning a source model (e.g., from CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100), then initialize that pruned structure either with the late-reset weights $\theta_k$ (lottery-ticket form) or with the fully trained source weights $\theta_i$, then fine-tune each initialization on a target non-natural dataset (example shown: Human-LBA) and compare final accuracy and robustness across pruning fractions.
Fig. 4

Report the empirical finding: models initialized with fully trained source weights $f(x;m\odot\theta_i)$ generally perform worse and are less robust to pruning than lottery-ticket late-reset initializations $f(x;m\odot\theta_k)$ when both are fine-tuned on the same target dataset. This behavior is reported for examples where $f(x;m\odot\theta_i)$ models trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 and fine-tuned on Human-LBA are shown to perform worse overall and to be less robust to pruning than the corresponding $f(x;m\odot\theta_k)$ lottery tickets.
Fig. 4

Provide the interpretation given in the paper: since $f(x;m\odot\theta_i)$ (pruned-but-fully-trained initializations) perform worse than $f(x;m\odot\theta_k)$ (late-reset lottery-ticket initializations) on the target, the inferior performance of natural-image tickets relative to target tickets in some datasets is not attributable to the weight re-initialization step (i.e., it is not due to resetting weights at $k$ rather than keeping final trained weights), but rather reflects a genuine difference in inductive bias and transferability between source and target tickets.

Conclude that, for transfer to a target non-natural dataset, the lottery-ticket form $f(x;m\odot\theta_k)$ yields higher final accuracy and greater robustness to high pruning rates than the same pruned structure initialized with final trained source weights $f(x;m\odot\theta_i)$, consistent with the experimental comparisons presented.

Describe the experimental question and the specific inter-target transfer tests: evaluate whether winning-ticket initializations discovered on a non-natural source dataset that is closely related to the target (e.g., Human-LBA → Mouse-LBA within live-blood-analysis, Artist-Classification-1 → Artist-Classification-2 within art classification) yield better performance or robustness when fine-tuned on the target than winning tickets obtained from unrelated natural-image sources.

Explain the observed results for the live-blood-analysis pair: when fine-tuning Human-LBA tickets on Mouse-LBA, the authors found that Human-LBA tickets perform just as well as Mouse-LBA tickets and are more robust to large pruning rates; this observation is reported in the central plots of the additional-studies figure and is explicitly described in the text discussing cross-non-natural transfers.

Explain the observed results for the art-classification pair: when fine-tuning tickets from Artist-Classification-1 onto Artist-Classification-2 (and reciprocally), the authors observed that Artist-Classification-1 tickets can outperform Artist-Classification-2 tickets when transferred, indicating that transferring between related non-natural datasets can yield better or comparable accuracy and improved robustness relative to transferring natural-image tickets; this result is also reported in the central plots of the additional-studies figure and in the Results text.
Fig. 4

Relate these findings to the contrast with natural-image tickets: the authors explicitly state that transferring winning tickets between related non-natural datasets yields better or comparable final accuracy and improved robustness to pruning compared to transferring unrelated natural-image tickets (i.e., tickets from CIFAR-10/100/Fashion-MNIST), and cite the Human-LBA → Mouse-LBA and Artist-Classification-1 ↔ Artist-Classification-2 experiments as empirical evidence.
Fig. 4

Conclude that, based on the presented cross-domain fine-tuning experiments, transferring winning-ticket initializations between related non-natural datasets is beneficial: it yields equal or better final accuracy on the target and improved robustness under extreme sparsity compared to transferring from unrelated natural-image sources, as demonstrated by the reported transfer experiments.

State the experimental manipulation used to probe the effect of source dataset size on ticket robustness: for a given target dataset, generate winning tickets by performing the same iterative pruning and late-reset procedure on source training data subsets obtained by reducing the original training data by 75%, 50% and 25% (i.e., using 25%, 50%, 75% of the original training set), then fine-tune the resulting tickets on the target and measure performance across pruning fractions; the specific claim highlights the 25% case.

Report the empirical observation from the reduced-data experiments: the performance-vs-sparsity curves for winning tickets obtained using only 25% of the training set are "just as stable" under increasing pruning as the curves for winning tickets obtained on the full training set, meaning that robustness to extreme pruning (the rate at which performance degrades as pruning fraction increases) is similar between tickets found on 25% of the data and those found on the full dataset. This observation is stated in the Results text and illustrated by the last row of the additional-studies figure.
Fig. 4

Report the accompanying caveat about final accuracy: although the robustness to pruning is similar for tickets found on 25% of the data, their final test accuracy on the target is lower than that of tickets discovered with the full training set; i.e., reduced-data tickets are equally stable but have reduced peak performance. This explicit trade-off is reported in the Results description of the size-of-training-set study.
Fig. 4

Conclude that the stability of lottery-ticket performance under high pruning does not strongly depend on the size of the training set used to discover the ticket (tickets found on only 25% of training data yield similar robustness curves), but that the peak test accuracy achievable after fine-tuning is reduced when tickets are discovered from smaller training sets; this conclusion is directly drawn by the authors from the reduced-data experiments and their visualization.

open_questions.content: The study leaves several empirical and methodological issues open. First, the paper reports domain-dependent transferability (natural→art transfers well; natural→biomedical less so) but does not identify the mechanistic causes: it remains unresolved how specific distributional differences (e.g., texture/statistics, imaging pipeline artifacts, biological morphology) determine whether a natural-image ticket contains transferable inductive biases for a given non-natural target. Second, the computational cost and practical strategies for discovering tickets that are broadly reusable across many non-natural targets remain open: the work reuses tickets from a small set of sources (CIFAR-10/100, Fashion-MNIST) and per-target discovery, but it is not resolved how to amortize ticket-discovery cost at scale or whether scalable ticket-finding algorithms exist that avoid repeated full training. Third, the experiments are limited to ResNet-50 and classification tasks; it is an open question whether the findings extend to other architectures and to other computer-vision tasks such as localization and segmentation (including biomedical segmentation), and to other modalities. Fourth, although training a ticket on reduced source-data preserves robustness but reduces peak accuracy, the relationship between source-data size, ticket sparsity level, and obtainable target accuracy has not been characterized quantitatively across regimes, leaving open how much source data is minimally required to obtain a ticket that yields near-optimal transfer performance. Finally, the study conjectures (but does not prove) that the poorer transfer to some biomedical datasets arises because those images are further from natural images than artworks are; formally testing this conjecture and deriving predictive measures of cross-domain ticket transferability remain open problems.
